issue.title: `PluginManager#hasPlugin` reports different results for actively-being-applied plugins depending on whether the target plugin has a `withPlugin` waiting on it
issue.body:
### Current Behavior

In the case where one plugin, plugin `x`, applies another plugin (`y`), usually a check from `y` for `pluginManager.hasPlugin("x")` will return true, even though `x` is still actively applying. Several projects in the wild make use of this, applying some (internal) plugin with shared behavior from each of two (public API) plugins, and then the internal plugin configures its behavior based on which plugin applied it, using `hasPlugin` to check for the presence of one or both public plugins.

However, if some other plugin, applied before `x`, calls `pluginManager.withPlugin("x") {}`, then any call to `hasPlugin("x")` will return false until `x` _finishes_ applying.

### Expected Behavior

The behavior of `hasPlugin` should consistently report one either "this plugin has started applying" or "this plugin has completed applying", instead of the current behavior in which which of those is reported depends on whether anything is waiting on the plugin to apply.

### Context (optional)

The root cause of this is some annoying details of the impl of `DefaultPluginManager`: `withPlugin` calls `pluginsForId`, which creates a domain container set of plugins with the given ID and adds a non-lazy callback to it. `hasPlugin` also calls `pluginsForId`, and checks whether the returned set is empty.

Thus, in the event that `withPlugin` is called first, there is a domain set for that id in the `idMappings` map backing `pluginsForId` by the time `hasPlugin` is called, and that set is returned as is, and is empty. The plugin is only added to this set in the callback at the end of `addPlugin` to `adder`, after it has finished applying.

When `hasPlugin` is called first, no set exists in the `idMappings` map, so `pluginsForId` creates one and populates it from the `plugins` map, which already contain the plugin in question -- this is populated before the plugin ever starts applying, in `addPluginInternal`.

### Self-contained Reproducer Project

https://github.com/lukebemish/gradle-issue-reproducer-withplugin-ordering-bug

### Gradle version

9.7.0

issue.title: No worker line is shown in the console for some configuration work
issue.body:
### Current Behavior

Before the tasks run, some work is done with no worker line:

- on every build with the configuration cache, the inputs of the configuration cache entry are checked;
- the `projectsLoaded`, `projectsEvaluated` and `taskGraph.whenReady` listeners of each build are run;
- after a change of a version catalog, or with an empty Gradle user home, the dependency accessors of the catalog are generated, and the type-safe project accessors when this feature is enabled.

While this work is done, only the status bar is shown, with `INITIALIZING` or `CONFIGURING` and the timer. When this work takes long, users can think that the build is stuck.

Example with a value source of 3 s, and a `projectsEvaluated` listener and a `whenReady` listener of 3 s each, with the configuration cache.

First build, with a configuration cache miss:

```
time after client start   console
 0.5 s                    │···············│ 0% CONFIGURING [90ms]
                          > root project
 3.5 s                    │███████████████│ 100% CONFIGURING [3s]
                          > IDLE
 8.5 s                    │███████████████│ 100% CONFIGURING [8s]
                          > IDLE
 9.5 s                    BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 9s
```

Second build, with a configuration cache hit:

```
time after client start   console
 1.0 s                    │···············│ 0% INITIALIZING [700ms]
 3.3 s                    │···············│ 0% INITIALIZING [3s]
 3.4 s                    BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 3s
```


### Expected Behavior

While each of these runs, a worker line is shown for it. For example:

```
> Checking configuration cache fingerprint
> Running projects loaded listeners
> Running projects evaluated listeners
> Running task graph ready listeners
> Generating dependency accessors for 'libs'
> Generating project accessors
```

For the work of an included build, the path of the build is shown first, as in `> :plugins > Running projects evaluated listeners`.

### Context (optional)

During the check of the configuration cache inputs, value sources are run again, and the files read during the configuration are checked. This is done on every configuration cache hit. The listeners contain user code. The accessors of a version catalog are generated and compiled.

A related report is #26154, where `100% CONFIGURING` and `> IDLE` were shown for minutes.


### Self-contained Reproducer Project

1. Create `settings.gradle.kts`:

   ```kotlin
   rootProject.name = "configuration-work"
   ```

2. Create `gradle.properties`:

   ```
   org.gradle.configuration-cache=true
   ```

3. Create `build.gradle.kts`:

   ```kotlin
   abstract class SlowValue : ValueSource<String, ValueSourceParameters.None> {
       override fun obtain(): String {
           Thread.sleep(3000)
           return "value"
       }
   }

   providers.of(SlowValue::class) {}.get()

   gradle.projectsEvaluated { Thread.sleep(3000) }
   gradle.taskGraph.whenReady { Thread.sleep(3000) }

   tasks.register("work")
   ```

4. Run the build twice with the rich console:

   ```
   gradle --console=rich work
   gradle --console=rich work
   ```

   In the first build, `100% CONFIGURING` is shown for 6 s after the configuration of the root project, with only `> IDLE` below it. In the second build, `0% INITIALIZING` is shown for 3 s, with no worker line.

9.8.1

issue.body:

If I copy my project folder with existing configuration cache entries in `.gradle/configuration-cache`, the entries are reused in the new location. issue.title: The progress bar shows replacement characters on the Linux console
issue.body:
### Current Behavior

On the Linux text console with a UTF-8 locale, Gradle draws the Unicode progress bar. The console fonts do not have the eighth blocks `▏ ▎ ▍ ▋ ▊ ▉` that the bar uses at the edge of the done part, so this cell shows the replacement glyph of the font, or `?`. With the reproducer below, after 2 tasks:

```
│███?···········│ 22% EXECUTING [2s]
```

### Expected Behavior

The bar is drawn with characters that the console fonts have, such as the ASCII bar:

```
[###............] 22% EXECUTING [2s]
```

### Context (optional)

None of the default console fonts of Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, RHEL and kbd has these characters, nor has the built-in kernel font. This was checked in their Unicode tables with `psfxtable`. `--console-unicode=disable` is a workaround.

Related: #35537, #37177

### Self-contained Reproducer Project

1. Create `settings.gradle.kts` with `rootProject.name = "progress"`.
2. Create `build.gradle.kts`:

   ```kotlin
   val steps = (1..8).map { i ->
       tasks.register("step$i") {
           doLast { Thread.sleep(1_000) }
       }
   }
   tasks.register("work") { dependsOn(steps) }
   ```

3. On a text console, for example after Ctrl+Alt+F3, run `gradle --console=rich work`.

issue.title: Show how long worker lines have run in the console
issue.body:
### Expected Behavior

Once the work of a worker line has run for 10 s, the line ends with how long it has run, in the format of the timer of the status bar. For example, with a task that runs for 30 s:

```
│···············│ 0% EXECUTING [14s]
> :work  13s
```

The time is the one of the deepest work shown on the line. For a test task, it is the time of the current test class, not of the task:

```
> :test > Executing test FooTest  1m 5s
```

Shorter work shows no time, so most lines do not change.


### Current Behavior (optional)

A worker line shows what runs, but not for how long. Only the timer of the status bar grows, and it gives the time of the whole build.

Example with a task that runs for 30 s:

```
time after client start   console
 3 s                      │···············│ 0% EXECUTING [2s]
                          > :work
15 s                      │···············│ 0% EXECUTING [14s]
                          > :work
29 s                      │···············│ 0% EXECUTING [28s]
                          > :work
```

1. Create `settings.gradle.kts`:

   ```kotlin
   rootProject.name = "slow-work"
   ```

2. Create `build.gradle.kts`:

   ```kotlin
   tasks.register("work") {
       doLast {
           Thread.sleep(30_000)
       }
   }
   ```

3. Run the build with the rich console:

   ```
   gradle --console=rich work
   ```

   For 30 s, only `> :work` is shown.

### Context

When a build seems stuck, users cannot see which work holds it up. A hung task, test class or download looks the same as one that has just started. In a parallel build, several worker lines are shown, and none of them tells how long its work has run. Today, users have to wait for the end of the build and read a Build Scan or the `--profile` report, or take a thread dump of the daemon.

issue.title: Deprecate starting external processes at configuration time outside of ProviderFactory.{java}exec or ValueSource
issue.body:
Starting an external process at configuration time should emit a deprecation warning even when the configuration cache is **not** enabled.

With the configuration cache on, this is already reported as an error:

> Starting an external process '<command>' during configuration time is unsupported.

With the configuration cache off, the same code runs silently — the only trace is the lack of an optional end-of-build "promo" nudge suggesting the user try the configuration cache. There is no deprecation and nothing that pushes build authors to migrate.

As we move toward the configuration cache being on by default, behavior that is unsupported with CC on should be deprecated ahead of time, so that build and plugin authors get a clear, actionable warning during the grace period rather than discovering a hard failure only once CC becomes the default.

Given the impact and the timeline for Gradle 10, we should not aim to elevate this to an error there.

## Expected behavior

Calling these APIs at configuration time emits a deprecation warning when configuration cache is not enabled:
- Gradle's exec APIs: `ExecOperations.exec` / `ExecOperations.javaexec` and the underlying exec spec actions
- `java.lang.ProcessBuilder.start()` and `ProcessBuilder.startPipeline(...)`
- `java.lang.Runtime.exec(...)` (all overloads)
- Groovy process helpers: `String.execute(...)`, `String[].execute(...)`, `List.execute(...)` (`ProcessGroovyMethods`)

issue.title: `embedded-kotlin` warns on the Kotlin Gradle Plugin version, not on the Kotlin compiler version
issue.body:
### Current Behavior

The `embedded-kotlin` plugin compares the version of the applied Kotlin Gradle Plugin with the Kotlin version embedded in Gradle. When the two versions differ, the plugin logs `WARNING: Unsupported Kotlin plugin version.`. The `kotlin-dsl` plugin applies `embedded-kotlin`, so build logic projects also get this warning.

The comparison reads `getKotlinPluginVersion()` in [`EmbeddedKotlinPlugin.kt:45`](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/blob/b700dade3bfd82368004732e0690d98c077324bc/platforms/core-configuration/kotlin-dsl-plugins/src/main/kotlin/org/gradle/kotlin/dsl/plugins/embedded/EmbeddedKotlinPlugin.kt#L45). This function returns the version of the Kotlin Gradle Plugin. It does not return the version of the Kotlin compiler that compiles the code. A build selects that compiler with the [`kotlinExtension.compilerVersion`](https://kotlinlang.org/api/kotlin-gradle-plugin/kotlin-gradle-plugin-api/org.jetbrains.kotlin.gradle.dsl/-kotlin-top-level-extension/compiler-version.html) property.

As a result, the warning is wrong in both directions. The attached reproducer shows both, with Gradle 9.7.0 and its embedded Kotlin 2.4.0.

**Case A: no warning, and the build fails.** The applied Kotlin Gradle Plugin is 2.4.0, and the compiler is 2.3.21:

```
--- case-a ---
Kotlin embedded in Gradle : 2.4.0
Applied Kotlin plugin     : 2.4.0
Kotlin compiler           : 2.3.21

e: java.lang.NoSuchFieldError: Class org.jetbrains.kotlin.config.CompilerConfigurationKey does not have member field 'org.jetbrains.kotlin.config.CompilerConfigurationKey$Companion Companion'

* What went wrong:
Execution failed for task ':compilePluginsBlocks' (registered by plugin class 'org.gradle.kotlin.dsl.plugins.precompiled.PrecompiledScriptPlugins').
> A failure occurred while executing org.jetbrains.kotlin.compilerRunner.btapi.BuildToolsApiCompilationWork
   > Compilation error. See log for more details
```

Gradle logs no warning. The compiler plugins of the `kotlin-dsl` plugin are version 2.4.0, and the Kotlin 2.3.21 compiler cannot load them. This is the exact risk that the warning must report. The same build without a `compilerVersion` value compiles without an error.

**Case B: a warning, and the build works.** The applied Kotlin Gradle Plugin is 2.4.10, and the compiler is 2.4.0:

```
WARNING: Unsupported Kotlin plugin version.
--- case-b ---
Kotlin embedded in Gradle : 2.4.0
Applied Kotlin plugin     : 2.4.10
Kotlin compiler           : 2.4.0

BUILD SUCCESSFUL
```

Gradle logs the warning, but the compiler is the one that Gradle expects. The warning is noise.


### Expected Behavior

The warning informs the user about one risk: the code compiles with a Kotlin compiler that differs from the compiler that Gradle expects. `compilerVersion` is the source of truth for that compiler version. Gradle compares `kotlinExtension.compilerVersion` with `embeddedKotlinVersion`, and logs the warning only when these two values differ.

Points to decide:

- `compilerVersion` is experimental in Kotlin Gradle Plugin 2.4.x. It needs two opt-in annotations: `@ExperimentalKotlinGradlePluginApi` and `@ExperimentalBuildToolsApi`. Gradle must accept this dependency on an experimental API.
- `compilerVersion` is a `Property<String>`. An eager read finalizes the value and stops later configuration of the property. The plugin does this comparison at apply time, so the new comparison must read the value lazily.
- The Kotlin documentation says that a `compilerVersion` value only has an effect when the Gradle property `kotlin.compiler.runViaBuildToolsApi` is `true`. The default value of the property is the version of the Kotlin Gradle Plugin, so builds without this property keep the current behavior.
- The property exists since Kotlin Gradle Plugin 2.1.20. A build can apply an older version, where this property is absent. Then the plugin must use `getKotlinPluginVersion()` as a default value, or Gradle must raise the minimum supported version.


### Context (optional)

This comes from a direct report by JetBrains on 2026-08-10. Users see the warning in projects that combine build logic with a recent version of the Kotlin Gradle Plugin. The warning is noise when the compiler version matches the Kotlin version embedded in Gradle.

### Self-contained Reproducer Project

The attached archive `kotlin-dsl-compiler-version-warning.zip` contains a Gradle wrapper for 9.7.0, a `README.md`, and two independent builds.

[kotlin-dsl-compiler-version-warning.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30975210/kotlin-dsl-compiler-version-warning.zip)

Run the two cases:

```
./gradlew -p case-a build
./gradlew -p case-b build
```

Case A fails and logs no warning. Case B succeeds and logs the warning.

Both builds set `kotlin.compiler.runViaBuildToolsApi=true` in `gradle.properties`, because `compilerVersion` only has an effect with this Gradle property. The build script of case A is:

```kotlin
import org.jetbrains.kotlin.buildtools.api.ExperimentalBuildToolsApi
import org.jetbrains.kotlin.gradle.ExperimentalKotlinGradlePluginApi

plugins {
    `kotlin-dsl`
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

// Compile with a Kotlin compiler that differs from the Kotlin version embedded in Gradle
@OptIn(ExperimentalKotlinGradlePluginApi::class, ExperimentalBuildToolsApi::class)
fun useOldCompiler() = kotlin {
    compilerVersion.set("2.3.21")
}
useOldCompiler()
```

Case B is the same, with `kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.10"` added to the `plugins` block, and with `compilerVersion` set to `embeddedKotlinVersion`.


### Gradle version

9.7.0. The check is also unchanged on `master` (9.8.0, embedded Kotlin 2.4.10), and it exists in earlier releases too.

issue.title: Deprecate implicit opt-in into Parallel Tooling Model Building
issue.body:
Context:
- https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/35996

---

We can make `org.gradle.parallel` and `org.gradle.parallel.tooling` independent options in a major Gradle release.

However, before we do that, we should warn users about the change, and do it much in advance, given the breadth of the adoption for the `org.gradle.parallel` property.

One strategy we can apply is to deprecate not being explicit about the PMF option if PE option is enabled.

In other words, starting from some Gradle version, we issue a deprecation, when we detect `org.gradle.parallel=true` in the build, while no explicit value for `org.gradle.parallel.tooling` is provided. To avoid the deprecation, all the users have to do is either enable or disable the PMF property explicitly.

issue.body:

When two tasks in parallel send a set of similar problems, the Gradle Problems API loses some of the events for these tasks - one task will show a subset of reported problems, and another one will show another non-intersecting subset.

For example:

issue.title: Running Worker API work actions are not shown in the console
issue.body:
### Current Behavior

When a task submits work actions with the Worker API, no worker line is shown for the running work actions. While they run, only the line of the task is shown, such as `> :work`. When this work takes long, users cannot see which work actions run.

Example with a task that submits two work actions of 3 s each, which run at the same time:

```
time after client start   console
 0.5 s                    │···············│ 0% EXECUTING [88ms]
                          > :work
 2.5 s                    │···············│ 0% EXECUTING [2s]
                          > :work
 3.5 s                    BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 3s
```

For tests, a worker line is shown for each running test class, and the number of completed tests is shown with the task:

```
> :test > 1 test completed
> :test > Executing test t.BTest
```


### Expected Behavior

While each work action runs, a worker line is shown for it, as for test classes, and the number of completed work actions is shown with the task:

```
> :work > 0 work actions completed
> :work > Executing work action Build_gradle$SlowAction
> :work > Executing work action Build_gradle$SlowAction
```

When the task does work of its own with a worker line, such as `> :work > Resolve dependencies of …`, this line is shown in place of the line of the task, as today.

### Context (optional)

_No response_

### Self-contained Reproducer Project

1. Create `settings.gradle.kts`:

   ```kotlin
   rootProject.name = "work-actions"
   ```

2. Create `build.gradle.kts`:

   ```kotlin
   abstract class SlowAction : WorkAction<WorkParameters.None> {
       override fun execute() = Thread.sleep(3000)
   }

   abstract class Work : DefaultTask() {
       @get:Inject
       abstract val workerExecutor: WorkerExecutor

       @TaskAction
       fun run() {
           val queue = workerExecutor.noIsolation()
           queue.submit(SlowAction::class.java) {}
           queue.submit(SlowAction::class.java) {}
       }
   }

   tasks.register<Work>("work")
   ```

3. Run the build with the rich console:

   ```
   gradle --console=rich work
   ```

   While the two work actions run, only `> :work` is shown for 3 s, and no worker line is shown for the work actions.

issue.title: Rich console timer is less than the duration in the build summary
issue.body:
### Current Behavior

The timer on the status bar of the rich console is started when the `Run build` build operation is started in the daemon. The duration in the build summary is measured from the start of the client JVM.

As a result, the time to start the client is not included in the timer value. When a new daemon is started, the time to start the daemon is not included either. Thus, the timer value is less than the duration in the build summary.

Example after `gradle --stop`, for a build with a task of 3 s:

```
time after client start   console
 1.0 s                    │···············│ 0% INITIALIZING [89ms]
 1.5 s                    │···············│ 0% CONFIGURING [589ms]
 1.9 s                    │···············│ 0% EXECUTING [989ms]
 4.0 s                    │···············│ 0% EXECUTING [3s]
 4.9 s                    BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 4s
```

The status bar is shown first at 1.0 s after the start of the client. At that time, the timer value is `[89ms]`. With an empty Gradle user home, the difference was 2.5 s.

When the daemon is already started, the difference is the time to start the client. The first frame is shown at 0.5 s after the start of the client, and the timer value is `[81ms]`.


### Expected Behavior

The timer value is the time since the start of the build, as for the build summary.

In the example above, the timer value of the first frame is `[1s]`. At the end of the build, the timer value is `[4s]`, and the duration in the build summary is `4s`.


### Context (optional)

The timer value and the duration in the build summary are both the duration of the build. With a new daemon, the two values are different by one second or more.

For a Build Scan, the start of the build is also the start of the client, as for the build summary.

In `BuildStatusRenderer`, the timer is started from the timestamp of the first build operation that is received. This TODO comment is in the code: `TODO - should use BuildRequestMetaData to determine the build start time`.

### Self-contained Reproducer Project

1. Create `settings.gradle.kts`:

   ```kotlin
   rootProject.name = "timer-check"
   ```

2. Create `build.gradle.kts`:

   ```kotlin
   tasks.register("slow") { doLast { Thread.sleep(3000) } }
   ```

3. Stop the Gradle daemons:

   ```
   gradle --stop
   ```

4. Run the build with the rich console:

   ```
   gradle --console=rich slow
   ```

5. Compare the timer value on the status bar with the duration in the build summary.

   The first timer value is less than 100 ms, but the command was started approximately 1 s before. The last timer value is approximately 1 s less than the duration in the build summary.

6. To see the time of each frame, stop the daemons again and record the build with asciinema:

   ```
   asciinema rec --command "gradle --console=rich slow" timer.cast
   ```

`org.gradle.configuration-cache.inputs.unsafe.ignore.file-system-checks` is a temporary Configuration Cache opt-out introduced in Gradle 8.3.
It restores the earlier behavior where file system checks such as `File.exists()` and `File.isFile()` on the listed paths are not tracked as configuration inputs.

It has always been documented as temporary, but using it produces no warning, so builds that set it have no signal that it is going away.

- [ ] Define the major version in which the property is removed
- [ ] Add a deprecation warning when the property is defined
- [ ] Add an entry to the upgrade guide
- [ ] Update all documentation references to point out the property is on its way out

issue.title: `signing.sign(publication)` resolves version-mapped classpaths at configuration time in 9.8.0-M1, breaking later `dependencies {}` blocks
issue.body:
# Current Behavior

Since Gradle 9.8.0-M1, calling `signing.sign(mavenPublication)` on a publication that uses `versionMapping { fromResolutionResult() }` eagerly resolves the mapped configurations (e.g. `compileClasspath`) **while `sign()` is being called**, i.e. during project configuration.

Resolving the project's own `compileClasspath` builds the local component and marks the project's consumable configurations (`apiElements`, `runtimeElements`, …) as observed. Any dependency declared afterwards in the same project fails with:

```
Cannot mutate the dependencies of configuration ':api' after the configuration's child configuration ':apiElements' was published as a variant. After a configuration has been observed, it should not be modified.
```

This is particularly painful when signing is configured by a convention plugin applied in `plugins {}`: the plugin runs before the script body, so every `dependencies {}` block in the build script fails. This broke publishing in the Gradle build itself (`:kotlin-dsl-plugins:publishPlugins` and the nightly promotion build) as soon as the wrapper was bumped to 9.8.0-M1. Locally it goes unnoticed because signing is only enabled when the signing key env vars are present (CI).

Even when no later mutation happens, resolving classpaths at configuration time for every signed publication is a performance regression and is incompatible with the lazy-configuration model.

# Expected Behavior

`signing.sign(publication)` should not resolve any configuration. It worked lazily in 9.7.0 (same reproducer passes).

# Context

Root cause, as far as I can tell from stack traces (full trace below):

1. `Sign.sign(Publication)` → `publicationInternal.allPublishableArtifacts(artifact -> isNoSignatureArtifact(artifact))` → `artifact.getFile()` — this has always been eager.
2. For the POM artifact, `SingleOutputTaskMavenArtifact.getFile()` does `task.getOutputs().getFiles().getSingleFile()` on `generatePomFileFor<Pub>Publication`, which visits *all* task properties via `TaskPropertyUtils.visitProperties`.
3. New in 9.8.0-M1: commit `23d63d19cdf` "Declare input annotations for MavenPom" made `GenerateMavenPom#getPom()` / `MavenPomInternal#getDependencies()` (and other members) `@Nested`. The property walker now unpacks the nested `Provider<MavenPomDependencies>`.
4. That provider is `DefaultMavenPublication` → `DefaultDependencyCoordinateResolverFactory`, which is built from `configuration.getIncoming().getResolutionResult().getRootComponent().zip(getRootVariant(), …)` for the version-mapped configurations → resolution happens right there.

# Steps to Reproduce

Self-contained, single-project Kotlin DSL build:

`settings.gradle.kts`
```kotlin
rootProject.name = "signing-repro"
```

`build.gradle.kts`
```kotlin
plugins {
    `java-library`
    `maven-publish`
    signing
}

group = "org.example"
version = "1.0"

publishing {
    publications {
        create<MavenPublication>("maven") {
            from(components["java"])
            versionMapping {
                usage("java-api") { fromResolutionResult() }
            }
        }
    }
}

signing {
    useInMemoryPgpKeys("not-a-real-key", "not-a-real-passphrase")
    sign(publishing.publications["maven"])
}

// Fails on 9.8.0-M1: compileClasspath was already resolved by signing.sign() above
dependencies {
    api("com.google.guava:guava:33.0.0-jre")
}
```

Run `gradle help`.

- Gradle 9.7.0: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`
- Gradle 9.8.0-M1:
  ```
  * Where:
  Build file '…/build.gradle.kts' line: 28

  * What went wrong:
  Cannot mutate the dependencies of configuration ':api' after the configuration's child configuration ':apiElements' was published as a variant. After a configuration has been observed, it should not be modified.
  ```
- Gradle 9.8.0-M1 with the `versionMapping {}` block removed: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` (so the resolution-backed POM dependencies provider is the trigger).

Stack trace of the configuration-time resolution (captured with an init script adding `configurations.configureEach { incoming.beforeResolve { Thread.dumpStack() } }`, trimmed):

```
CONFIG-TIME RESOLVE ::compileClasspath
	at org.gradle.api.internal.artifacts.configurations.DefaultConfiguration.resolveGraphIfRequired(DefaultConfiguration.java:654)
	at org.gradle.api.internal.artifacts.configurations.DefaultConfiguration$ResolverResultsResolutionResultProvider.getValue(DefaultConfiguration.java:636)
	at org.gradle.api.internal.artifacts.result.DefaultResolutionResult.lambda$getRootComponent$0(DefaultResolutionResult.java:67)
	... (MergeProvider / FlatMapProvider / TransformBackedProvider chain from DefaultDependencyCoordinateResolverFactory)
	at org.gradle.api.internal.provider.DefaultProperty.calculateValueFrom(DefaultProperty.java:158)
	at org.gradle.api.internal.provider.AbstractMinimalProvider.getOrNull(AbstractMinimalProvider.java:105)
	at org.gradle.internal.properties.annotations.AbstractTypeMetadataWalker$InstanceTypeMetadataWalker.lambda$walkNestedProvider$0(AbstractTypeMetadataWalker.java:139)
	at org.gradle.internal.properties.annotations.AbstractTypeMetadataWalker$InstanceTypeMetadataWalker.walkNestedProvider(AbstractTypeMetadataWalker.java:138)
	... (walking @Nested GenerateMavenPom#getPom() -> @Nested MavenPomInternal#getDependencies())
	at org.gradle.api.internal.tasks.TaskPropertyUtils.visitAnnotatedProperties(TaskPropertyUtils.java:58)
	at org.gradle.api.internal.tasks.TaskPropertyUtils.visitProperties(TaskPropertyUtils.java:35)
	at org.gradle.api.internal.tasks.DefaultTaskOutputs.getFileProperties(DefaultTaskOutputs.java:157)

	at org.gradle.plugins.signing.Sign.isNoSignatureArtifact(Sign.java:221)
```

Workaround: defer the call, e.g. `afterEvaluate { signing.sign(publication) }`. This avoids the mutation error but still resolves the classpaths at configuration time.

Regression in 9.8.0-M1 (`gradle-9.8.0-milestone-1`). Works in 9.7.0. Introduced by `23d63d19cdf` ("Declare input annotations for MavenPom").

### Current Behavior

Given this `build.gradle.kts`:

```kotlin
tasks.register<Sync>("sync") {
  from(layout.projectDirectory.dir("in"))
  into(layout.projectDirectory.dir("out"))
}
```

And this folder structure (other files are empty):

```

├── settings.gradle.kts
├── in
│   └── foo.txt
└── out
```

- Run: `gradle sync`

```
├── build.gradle.kts
├── settings.gradle.kts
├── in
│   └── foo.txt
└── out
    └── foo.txt
```
- Delete: `rm in/foo.txt`
- Run: `gradle sync`

```
├── build.gradle.kts
├── settings.gradle.kts
├── in
└── out
    └── foo.txt
```

### Expected Behavior

After running `Sync` on the now empty `in` folder, an empty `out` folder is expected:

```
├── build.gradle.kts
├── settings.gradle.kts
├── in
└── out
```


### Context (optional)

The `Sync` task action does not run, because `> Task :sync NO-SOURCE`.

This is due to the configuration inherited from `AbstractCopyTask` which adds a `skipWhenEmpty()` [here](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/blob/aec782af05a4c94a3dec185903ef0b45acf99892/subprojects/core/src/main/java/org/gradle/api/tasks/AbstractCopyTask.java#L93).

issue.title: Compile avoidance misses a change of record component order
issue.body:
### Current Behavior

Gradle uses the extracted ABI of each compile classpath entry for compile avoidance.
The extractor drops every record component, so a change of the component order does
not change the hash. Gradle then keeps the consumer up to date.

A record pattern binds each variable to a component position. The consumer keeps the
old positions after the change, and it gives a wrong result.

The reproducer has a library with `record Point(int x, int y)` and a consumer with a
record pattern. A swap of the two components gives this output:

```
> Task :lib:compileJava
> Task :app:compileJava UP-TO-DATE
f(new Point(1, 2)) = 21
```

A clean build of the same sources prints 12.

The cause is in `platforms/core-configuration/java-api-extractor`. `ApiMemberSelector`
does not implement `visitRecordComponent`, so the extracted class holds an empty
`Record` attribute. Both component orders keep the same accessors, the same canonical
constructor and the same private fields, therefore the extracted bytes are equal.




### Expected Behavior

The extracted ABI holds the record components. A change of the component order changes
the hash, and Gradle recompiles the consumer. An incremental build gives the same
result as a clean build.

### Context (optional)

Stumbled upon this while looking at
* https://github.com/gradle/gradle/pull/38810

Related issues
* https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/38825
* https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/38827
* https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/38828


### Self-contained Reproducer Project

The attached `records-abi-repro.zip` holds a two-module build. The wrapper uses Gradle
9.7.0. Java 21 or later is necessary for the record pattern.

[records-abi-repro.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31025625/records-abi-repro.zip)

Run `./reproduce.sh`, or follow these steps:

1. Run `./gradlew :app:run`. The output is 12.
2. Run `cp lib/variants/Point-swapped.java lib/src/main/java/Point.java`.
3. Run `./gradlew :app:run`. Gradle reports `:app:compileJava UP-TO-DATE`, and the
   output is 21.
4. Run `./gradlew :app:clean :app:run`. The output is 12 again.

`new Point(1, 2)` always puts 1 in the first component and 2 in the second component.
The pattern always reads the first component and then the second component. The
correct output is therefore 12 for both component orders.



### Gradle version

9.7.0. Gradle 9.6.1 gives the same result.

issue.title: No worker line is shown in the console for the work at the end of the build
issue.body:
### Current Behavior

After the last task, more work is done before the end of the build:

- the flow actions are run;
- `close()` is called on the build services;
- with `--write-locks`, the dependency locks are written;
- with `--write-verification-metadata`, the verification metadata is written.

No worker line is shown for this work. Only the status bar is shown, with `100% EXECUTING` and the timer. When this work takes long, users can think that the build is stuck.

Example with a flow action of 3 s and a build service with a `close()` of 3 s, after a task of almost no time:

```
time after client start   console
 0.7 s                    │███████████████│ 100% EXECUTING [80ms]
 3.0 s                    │███████████████│ 100% EXECUTING [2s]
 6.0 s                    │███████████████│ 100% EXECUTING [5s]
 6.7 s                    BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 6s
```

### Expected Behavior

While each of these runs, a worker line is shown for it. For example:

```
> Flow action c.e.n.SlackNotificationAction
> Close build service 'cache' (c.e.CacheService)
> Write dependency locks for project ':app'
> Write dependency verification metadata
```

For the work of an included build, the path of the build is shown first, as in `> :plugins > Flow action …`.


### Context (optional)

Flow actions and `close()` contain user code, which can take long. The writing of verification metadata can include the download of signatures and keys. In a build with many projects, many lock files are written.

### Self-contained Reproducer Project

1. Create `settings.gradle.kts`:

   ```kotlin
   rootProject.name = "end-of-build"
   ```

2. Create `build.gradle.kts`:

   ```kotlin
   abstract class SlowService : BuildService<BuildServiceParameters.None>, AutoCloseable {
       override fun close() = Thread.sleep(3000)
   }

   abstract class SlowAction : FlowAction<FlowParameters.None> {
       override fun execute(parameters: FlowParameters.None) = Thread.sleep(3000)
   }

   abstract class FlowRegistration @Inject constructor(val flowScope: FlowScope)

   val service = gradle.sharedServices.registerIfAbsent("slow", SlowService::class) {}

   tasks.register("work") {
       usesService(service)
       doLast { service.get() }
   }

   objects.newInstance<FlowRegistration>().flowScope.always(SlowAction::class) {}
   ```

3. Run the build with the rich console:

   ```
   gradle --console=rich work
   ```

   After the task, the status bar is shown for 6 s, and no worker line is shown.


### Gradle version

9.8.1

issue.title: Old text is left at the end of the status bar in the console
issue.body:
### Current Behavior

Sometimes, output is written above the status bar, and more worker lines are added in the same update of the console.
Then the end of an old worker line can be left after the status bar.
The status bar is drawn again lower, on the row of an old worker line.
When this old line is longer than the status bar, its end is not erased.
This end is left until the area of the status bar and the worker lines is moved again.

Example with three tasks with long names, in parallel.
One line is written by `prepareTheEnvironmentOfTheParallelTasks`, and three tasks that depend on it are started when it is complete:

```
time after client start   console
 1.5 s                    │···············│ 0% EXECUTING [1s]
                          > :downloadTheDependenciesOfTheParallelTasks
                          > :generateTheSourcesOfTheParallelTasks
                          > :prepareTheEnvironmentOfTheParallelTasks
 2.5 s
                          > Task :prepareTheEnvironmentOfTheParallelTasks
                          Environment ready
                          │██▏············│ 14% EXECUTING [2s]lTasks
                          > :downloadTheDependenciesOfTheParallelTasks
                          > :generateTheSourcesOfTheParallelTasks
                          > :work1
                          > :work2
                          > :work3
 6.5 s
                          > Task :prepareTheEnvironmentOfTheParallelTasks
                          Environment ready
                          │██▏············│ 14% EXECUTING [6s]lTasks
                          > :downloadTheDependenciesOfTheParallelTasks
                          > :generateTheSourcesOfTheParallelTasks
                          > :work1
                          > :work2
                          > :work3
```

The text that is left depends on the order of the worker lines, for example `lTasks`, `lelTasks` or `sks`.
The same is seen with the prompt at the bottom of the terminal, and in a terminal with free rows below the prompt.

On master, the fingerprint check of the configuration cache is shown on a worker line since #39541.
Thus, the same is seen on each configuration cache hit with a slow fingerprint check.
`Reusing configuration cache.` is written on the row of the status bar, and the tasks are started in the same update:

```
Reusing configuration cache.
│···············│ 0% EXECUTING [3s]erprint
> :work1
> :work2
> :work3
```

### Expected Behavior

When a line is drawn on another row than before, the end of the row is erased:

```
> Task :prepareTheEnvironmentOfTheParallelTasks
Environment ready
│██▏············│ 14% EXECUTING [2s]
> :downloadTheDependenciesOfTheParallelTasks
> :generateTheSourcesOfTheParallelTasks
> :work1
> :work2
> :work3
```

### Context (optional)

The status bar and the worker lines are drawn in `MultiLineBuildProgressArea.redraw()`.
In an update, the area is moved down by the rows of new output, and rows are added for new worker lines.
Each line is compared with the old text of the line that is lower by the sum of these two numbers of rows.
The end of the row is erased if this old text was longer.
But the old text under a line is the text of the line that is lower by the rows of new output only.
Thus, when worker lines are added in the same update, the wrong lines are compared.

This comparison was added with the first version of the rich console, in 2017.

### Self-contained Reproducer Project

1. Create `settings.gradle.kts`:

   ```kotlin
   rootProject.name = "leftover"
   ```

2. Create `gradle.properties`, to run the tasks of the project in parallel:

   ```
   org.gradle.configuration-cache=true
   ```

3. Create `build.gradle.kts`:

   ```kotlin
   val prepare = tasks.register("prepareTheEnvironmentOfTheParallelTasks") {
       doLast {
           Thread.sleep(2000)
           println("Environment ready")
       }
   }

   val download = tasks.register("downloadTheDependenciesOfTheParallelTasks") {
       doLast { Thread.sleep(7000) }
   }

   val generate = tasks.register("generateTheSourcesOfTheParallelTasks") {
       doLast { Thread.sleep(7000) }
   }

   val work = (1..3).map { i ->
       tasks.register("work$i") {
           dependsOn(prepare)
           doLast { Thread.sleep(5000) }
       }
   }

   tasks.register("all") {
       dependsOn(work, download, generate)
   }
   ```

4. Run the build with the rich console, in a terminal of 80 columns:

   ```
   gradle all
   ```

   After `Environment ready`, the end of a worker line is shown at the end of the status bar until the build is complete.

9.8.1

issue.title: Support Kotlin `object` singletons in Configuration Cache Serializer
issue.body:
Given a custom kotlin Sealed class with some `object` implementations used in the Task Configuration state.

```kotlin
sealed class SealedObject {
  object A: SealedObject()
  object B: SealedObject()
}

abstract class FooTask : DefaultTask() {
  private val sealedObject: SealedObject = SealedObject.A

  @TaskAction
  fun action() {
        val a = when (sealedObject) {
            SealedObject.A -> "a"
            SealedObject.B -> "b"
            else -> "null"
        }
        println("Value of a=$a")
        println("Hashcode of enumVal: ${sealedObject.hashCode()}")
        println("HashCode of A: ${SealedObject.A.hashCode()}")
        println("HashCode of B: ${SealedObject.B.hashCode()}")
  }
}
```

### Expected Behavior
It is expected consistent task execution results with and without configuration cache.

### Current Behavior
When configuration cache is reused `FooTask.sealedObject` will have different hashCode than actual `SealedObject.A`
thus they will not be equal to each other. I.e. `FooTask.sealedObject === SealedObject.A` is FALSE.

```log
> Task :customTask
Value of a=null
Hashcode of enumVal: 115347557
HashCode of A: 486130174
HashCode of B: 331638854

...

Configuration cache entry reused.
```

### Context
It is well-known issue among Java serializers that create copies of object implementations of Kotlin's sealed classes.
In [Jackson](https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson-module-kotlin/issues/225) for example.

Reproducible on the current `master`

issue.title: Please document what the advantage is of having interfaces that implement `Named` for attributes
issue.body:
### Issue type

Missing information

### Problem description

What is the advantage of having interfaces that implement `Named` for attributes like `public interface Usage extends Named`?
I mean opposed to just having the attributes with type `String`.
In the module metadata they are just strings.
To set them you use the `String` constants in the interface.
You can also use any arbitrary other string.

So the only effect I can realize right now is, that it is more cumbersome to set the attributes by needing to use `objects.named` to create  the value instead of just setting a `String` as value.

https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/variant_attributes.html#sec:declaring_attributes

issue.title: Make it possible to publish version catalogs defined in settings.gradle
issue.body:
### Expected Behavior
It should be possible to publish a version catalog that is defined in _settings.gradle_ with the `dependencyResolutionManagement.versionCatalogs` DSL. 

### Context
The gradle project that contains the version catalog also contains code that uses the catalog (to do some sanity checks before publishing the catalog). However currently there does not seem to be any way to do this, as the _version-catalog_ plugin does not have any DSL to use an existing catalog for publishing. 
The only way I can think of right now is to use the .toml format and `from(file(...))`, but I am not sure this will even work (and we also loose the typesafe DSL this way of course).

issue.title: Files restored from the build cache are recorded with their size and last modified time swapped
issue.body:
When Gradle restores a task's outputs from the build cache, it records each restored file's size and last modified time the wrong way round. Anything that reads those values gets wrong numbers: a small jar restored from the cache reports a size of about 1.8 TB.

### Current behavior

`TarBuildCacheEntryPacker.unpackFile` calls `DefaultFileMetadata.file(output.getCount(), file.lastModified(), DIRECT)`, but the signature is `file(lastModified, length, accessType)`.
`BuildCacheStep` stores the resulting snapshots in the virtual file system, so a task that consumes a restored file picks them up in its input snapshot.

The swap came in with 7f3ba77fe8ac3afd15565036730df297c3b13f1d in Gradle 6.5. Nothing read these values until 9.6 added `VisitState.getLength()`.
On 9.6+ the Develocity plugin uses it for the size of each resolved artifact, which is how we noticed: in one build, the three jars restored from the cache showed up at about 1.79 TB each, while the other 1,338 sizes were correct.

### Expected behavior

The snapshot holds the file's real size and last modified time.

### Context

Up-to-date checks don't seem affected, since hashing reads fresh file metadata.
`isContentAndMetadataUpToDate` compares the full metadata and overlapping-outputs filtering uses it, so a cache-restored file sitting in another task's output directory might be counted as that task's output. I haven't verified that one.

### Steps to reproduce

Unpack a cache entry with `TarBuildCacheEntryPacker` and read the metadata of the returned `RegularFileSnapshot`: `getLength()` returns the last modified time. The linked PR adds a unit test for this.

### Gradle version

6.5 and later

issue.title: Usage of `Cached` in `DefaultJvmInstallationMetadata.capabilities` is  not thread-safe
issue.body:
### Issue type

Polishing

### Problem description

`org.gradle.internal.serialization.Cached` is not meant for multi-threaded usage. It can only honor the at-most-once semantics if used from a single thread. Also, multi-threaded usage may lead to unexpected runtime exceptions (we have seen NPEs, though those have been addressed [here](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/pull/31240)).

For infrastructure data, `CalculatedValue` is preferred. `Cached` should be used for model types only. 

Related issue: https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/31239


### Context (optional)

Via @adammurdoch :

> If we're seeing a problem with the toolchains stuff not being thread-safe, then we should fix it rather than add work arounds to `Cached`.
Specifically, if we're seeing problems with DefaultJvmInstallationMetadata I would make the capabilities field eager, so that the object becomes data only. I don't see any real benefit in making that field lazy.

issue.title: Clean up remaining org.gradle.unsafe.isolated-projects property usages
issue.body:
### Summary

The Isolated Projects properties were renamed and the `org.gradle.unsafe.*` names are now deprecated aliases:

- `org.gradle.unsafe.isolated-projects` → `org.gradle.isolated-projects`
- `org.gradle.unsafe.isolated-projects.diagnostics` → `org.gradle.isolated-projects.diagnostics`
- `org.gradle.unsafe.isolated-projects.dangerously-ignore-problems` → `org.gradle.isolated-projects.dangerously-ignore-problems`

Several places in the repository still use the old `unsafe` names. This issue tracks cleaning them up to use the current names.

Spun off from https://github.com/gradle/gradle/pull/37759#discussion_r3511384341 ("Drop `unsafe`. There are other places like this").

### Candidates to update

- `.teamcity/src/main/kotlin/projects/CheckProject.kt`
- `.teamcity/src/main/kotlin/projects/GradleBuildToolRootProject.kt`
- `build-logic/performance-testing/src/main/kotlin/gradlebuild/performance/tasks/BuildCommitDistribution.kt`
- `gradle.properties` (repo root)
- `platforms/core-configuration/configuration-cache/src/integTest/groovy/org/gradle/internal/cc/impl/isolated/IsolatedProjectsIntegrationTest.groovy`

### Needs per-file judgement

- `platforms/ide/tooling-api/src/crossVersionTest/.../r930|r940|r970/*.groovy` — cross-version tests may target older Gradle versions where only the `unsafe` name exists; verify before changing.
- `architecture/standards/0010-gradle-properties-naming.md` — uses the name as a naming-convention example; may be intentional.

### Must NOT change (they intentionally reference the deprecated name)

- `platforms/core-runtime/start-parameter/src/main/java/org/gradle/initialization/StartParameterBuildOptions.java` — defines `DEPRECATED_PROPERTY_NAME` for backwards-compatible handling.
- `platforms/documentation/docs/src/docs/userguide/releases/upgrading/upgrading_version_9.adoc` — documents the deprecation/rename.
- `platforms/documentation/docs/src/docs/release/notes.md` — release notes for the change.

### Notes

- The two docs snippets flagged in the PR review (`isolatedProjects/lifecycleApplyFalse` and `isolatedProjects/lifecycleSettingsPlugin` `gradle.properties`) are being fixed directly in #37759 and are not part of this cleanup.
- `git grep "org.gradle.unsafe.isolated-projects"` is a good starting point (~15 files at time of filing).
